4618.dq: Rumsen stress appears to fall predominantly on the first syllable of a word as in Mutsun (Okrand 1977).
4618.prule: Word-initial: primary stress on the first syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive (vowel length is phonemic and stated independently of stress in section 2). Evidence given is three Spanish loans (3 and 4 syllables) whose Spanish penultimate stress has shifted to the initial syllable, plus the parallel with Mutsun (Okrand 1977: 98).
4618.srule: Not mentioned in Kaufman 2009, section 3 "Stress", p. 40 (whole paper, pp. 39-45, read): the stress section is a single paragraph on word-initial (primary) stress; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described and the texts carry no stress marks.
4618.quote: Rumsen stress appears to fall predominantly on the first syllable of a word as in Mutsun (Okrand 1977). In regards to Mutsun, Okrand states that “the best evidence for word-initial stress comes from non-native vocabulary. If a loanword from Spanish has stress on a syllable other than that which is stressed in Spanish, the shift must be due to Mutsun stress patterns” (ibid.: 98). The same also seems to hold true for Rumsen, which also has Spanish loan words with the stress shifted to first syllable: púyyito ‘chicken’ from pollito; káwwayo ‘horse’ from caballo; and kásteyano ‘Spanish’ from cast…

4619.dq: Stress seems to be predictable based on tone plus rhythm of syllables within a phonological phrase.
4619.dloc: OPD p.3 (page 3), section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'; born-digital PDF fetched from the Internet Archive copy of sil.org
4619.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Tone is phonemic (four-way contrast on monosyllables: falling, rising, level, rising-falling; Pinyin-style marks, written only where needed). Stress is treated as non-contrastive and, with a hedge ('seems to be'), as predictable from tone together with the rhythm of syllables inside the phonological phrase; no position, weight or fixed-stress rule (quantity-insensitive) is given. Second-hand (Cahill 2011 on Newman & Petterson 1990): one accented syllable per phonological word anchors one of four melodies H/HL/LH/LHL; the accent falls on the final syllable, on the penult in about 8.5% of words.
4619.srule: Not mentioned in Petterson 1992 (Rumu OPD), p.3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' (whole 4-pp. OPD read): the only stress sentence derives stress from tone plus 'rhythm of syllables within a phonological phrase' and gives no secondary or rhythmic stress placement. Also not mentioned in Cahill 2011 sec. 2.5 or Donohue 1997 sec. 3.2.1 (tone only).

4620.tone: Two-tone language (High/Low) with distinctive vowel quantity; tone counted on moras. Stevick 1965 (FSI Kirundi Basic Course, Unit 1 note 1, pp. 11 and 13; text file, verified): 'In Kirundi however, as in most African languages, pitch has functions which it does not have in English.... Pitch, then, may be the only audible difference between two words of entirely different meanings. To say the same thing in technical terms, Kirundi has LEXICALLY SIGNIFICANT distinctions of pitch.' and 'In Kirundi, as in many other Bantu languages, the pitch phenomena are best described in terms of two tones, called LOW HIGH. Low tone is quite simple: its typical realization is as a level, relatively low pitch... As its name implies, high tone ordinarily involves the use of a relatively high pitch, but this pitch is not level.' The words 'stress' and 'accent' (prominence sense) do not occur in Stevick's 589-page text. tn.quote: Bien qu'il n'y ait que deux niveaux de hauteur essentiels (bas et haut), il y a trois tonèmes fondamentaux: ton bas, ton haut anté- rieur, ton haut postérieur . Le ton bas est tout entier au niveau bas ... le ton haut antérieur consiste essentiellement en une descente, précédée, si possible, d'une montée « préparatoire » de la syllabe précédente ... accent aigu (á, áa); le postérieur par accent circonflexe renversé dans le cas d'une voyelle brève (ă), par accent aigu sur la deuxiè- me lettre pour la ... voyelle longue (aá); le ton haut double par deux accents (áá)
tn.translation: Although there are only two essential pitch levels (low and high), there are three fundamental tonemes: low tone, anterior high tone, posterior high tone. The low tone is entirely at the low level ... the anterior high tone consists essentially of a fall, preceded, if possible, by a 'preparatory' rise on the preceding syllable ... [the anterior is marked by] acute accent (á, áa); the posterior by inverted circumflex on a short vowel (ă), by acute accent on the second letter for the ... long vowel (aá); the double high tone by two accents (áá)

Weight plays no role; the position is anchored to the root, not counted from the word edge.

4622.prule: Mobile, non-automatic (lexically determined) word stress: Kodzasov gives no placement rule for Rutul ('accent paradigms have not been studied'), only the general Dagestanian statement that word stress is always mobile and non-automatic and in most stress languages falls on one of the first two syllables; Kodzasov 2003:64 makes the window explicit for Rutul ('initially oriented stress which is displaced in the window of the first two syllables... can be handled now only by means of lexical marking'). The primary grammars, seen in excerpt, add a part-of-speech tendency inside the window: nouns as a rule on the second syllable from the beginning (Ibragimov 1978 §45, Mukhad dialect), verbs mostly on the first (Alekseev 1994:218). In Luchek Rutul the stressed syllable additionally carries one of four tonal accents (H, L, R, F).

II), i.e. a falling diphthong Vĭ/Vŭ of the type Carvalho lists on p. 7 (aĭ, aŭ, eĭ, éŭ, êŭ, óĭ, ôĭ, oŭ, uĭ, compared to Portuguese alfaia, pauta, ceia, chapéu, judeu, boia, joio, matou-a, aleluia; ex. dizêu 'dente'). Carvalho's syllable is (consonant or semivowel ĭ/ŭ) + (vowel or diphthong) (p. 11), so the diphthong is a two-element nucleus of one syllable.

4623.prule: Word 'accento tonico' on the penultimate syllable by default ('quasi sempre'), but on the final syllable when that syllable contains a diphthong whose second element is ĭ or ŭ (a falling diphthong, e.g. dizêu 'tooth'; p. 7 Obs. II: 'neste caso é esta a syllaba predominante'). A few other words are final-accented (dičiad̃iá 'day after tomorrow') and very few antepenultimate (sâb̃año 'six', tátuko 'father'); a penult-accented word moves its accent to its last syllable when joined to a following word (ŭape > ŭapé kamo 'good, better'; ukŭete > ukŭeté ŭoma 'has, is afraid'). Post-tonic vowels before a voiceless non-nasal consonant are whispered, almost inaudible (p. 6 Obs. I).

4623.tone: Carvalho 1890 never mentions tone (the word does not occur in the phonology). Every 20th-century description is tone-only and does not discuss stress: Angenot & Vincke 1977 (twelve ordered tone rules), Ntotila & Vincke 1986 (tonemes H and L, L marked, H most frequent; no accent/intensity statement), Nash 1994 (underlying L, default H, tone reversal relative to Proto-Bantu; short final vowels devoiced then deleted except u). Nash's only prominence remarks: fn 44 p. 269-270 'Even in contemporary Ruwund, syllables bearing abrupt-falling pitch patterns have a certain accent-like prominence, and as observed earlier, the overall pitch range employed is not very wide'; p. 272 'All nouns of pattern (e) appear to be borrowings from Swahili, a language with penultimate stress.' (contrasting Swahili with Ruwund, without stating that Ruwund lacks penultimate stress). Carvalho's 'accento tonico' and his acute/circumflex marks may in part be perceptions of the H/L tone contrast rather than stress; nothing in the modern sources confirms or denies penultimate stress.

4628.heavy: Long vowels: 'When long vowels appear, they usually bear primary stress or secondary stress... They bear the primary stress, when there are more than two syllables (including two syllables) in a word, and it falls on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable.' Closed syllables are not mentioned as heavy (syllables are open (C)V; the CVC/VC syllables created by word-final vowel dropping in rapid speech do not move stress, sec. 2.3.3). A sequence of two vowels is two syllable nuclei, and 'stress (if any) can fall on either vowel' (p. 34, citing Ting 1967:926).
4628.dflt: Penultimate in disyllables; penultimate or antepenultimate in longer words with no single default named by the author (free variation in some words); every stress-shift example in 2.18-2.19 and all light-syllable examples in 2.17 land the primary stress on the penult.
4628.prule: Non-contrastive primary stress confined to the final two-syllable window of the phonological word: penultimate in disyllables; penultimate or antepenultimate in words of three or more syllables, with free inter- and intra-speaker variation between the two positions in some words (sa.rí.a ~ sá.ri.a). A long vowel in the window 'usually' bears the primary stress, so antepenultimate when the antepenult is long (ɫúː.ɫu.ŋu, mɨ́ː.mɨ.a, máː.taː.ta); a long vowel outside the window usually takes secondary stress (pùː.si.á.mɨ), though not after rightward shift (puː.sì.a.mɨ́-ku). Suffixes and enclitics shift the primary stress rightward so that it stays penultimate/antepenultimate in the enlarged word (sà.kɨ.rá.ɫɨ -> sa.kɨ̀.ra.ɫɨ́=na); voice-marker prefixes do not shift it.
4628.srule: Secondary stress (non-contrastive, marked with a grave accent) only in words of four or more syllables; none in shorter words. Pan: only prefixes, not suffixes or enclitics, can carry it; his examples put it on the leftmost prefix when there is one (sàː-ɫa.má.r-a, kù-a-sa.ka-sá.ka.vɨ, kù-a-ŋa.ɫa.ŋa.ɫa=á.ku), otherwise two syllables to the left of the primary (à.rɨ.mɨ́.ɫɨ, sà.kɨ.rá.ɫɨ, pùː.si.á.mɨ, ŋà.ɫa.ŋá.ɫa). It shifts rightward with the primary when a suffix or enclitic attaches (sa.kɨ̀.ra.ɫɨ́=na, puː.sì.a.mɨ́-ku) and leftward onto an added prefix, leftward shift first; long vowels usually carry primary or secondary stress. One secondary stress per word in every example; no iterating rhythm is described.

4633.dq: The vocoids occurring in the mono- syllabic words are uniformly long; while in disyllabic, tri – syllabic and tetra- syllabic words (available a very few), the vocoids of the second syllable are long. Stress also is a co- occurring feature with the length, i.e., the syllables having long vocoids are always stressed.
4633.dloc: Section 2.3 'Major allophonics distributions', p. 459; examples pp. 459-465
4633.heavy: No phonological weight: 'The length is not phonemic.' Stress co-occurs with phonetic long vocoids, whose position is predictable (monosyllable; second syllable of 2-4 syllable words).
4633.prule: Stress is non-contrastive and rides on phonetic vowel length, which the sketch calls positional: a monosyllable is long and stressed; in words of two, three or four syllables the vowel of the second syllable is long and therefore stressed. Second syllable from the left, quantity-insensitive (length is not phonemic). The sketch's own transcriptions corroborate the placement: of the 205 acute-marked forms in the sketch, 68 are monosyllables and 137 are polysyllables (120 disyllables, 17 trisyllables, no tetrasyllable), and every polysyllable is marked on the second syllable, including trisyllables with an open second syllable ([ku:kú:ro] 'dog', [kAtá: ri] 'sugarcane', [pA:pi΄:ta] 'papaya', [bA:khÁ:ri] 'grain store'), with two deviations, [mo΄:Rhá] 'cane chair' (p. 468) and [ cÁ: n dá] 'donation' (p. 472), each marked on both syllables, evidently typographical slips. No tetrasyllable carries a mark, so the 4-syllable grid rests on the prose alone.

4638.heavy: Stated in morae: 'b）日本語に類似したモーラ型言語である。1モーラ：CV，V，C*の三種がある' (three mora types CV, V = second half of a long vowel, C* = coda /s, m, n, w, y, h/); '主アクセントは第2モーラにある … 但し，そのアクセントのあるべきモーラがVまたはC*であれば，その前のモーラにアクセントが移る'. Hence a bimoraic first syllable, CVV (kaa, niikah, yaanii) or CVC (pon, kahkemah), carries the accent; a light CV first syllable passes it to syllable 2. Hattori 1961: 4-5 likewise counts C1VV, C1VC2 and C1VC1V as two morae ('3者とも2モーラである。従ってC2はそれだけで1モーラをなす').
4638.dflt: second syllable (the 2nd mora) when the first syllable is light CV, regardless of the second syllable's own weight: sapa LH, cikah LH, ʔikuu LH, hekaci LHL, ʔarawan LHL, nisahta LHL, ʔuneeno LHL, hacikoo LHL (ings)
4638.prule: One culminative, non-contrastive pitch accent per word, placed on the 2nd mora; the accent retracts to the 1st mora when the 2nd mora is the second half of a long vowel (V) or a coda consonant (C*). In syllable terms: the accent (pitch peak) falls on the first syllable when it is heavy (CVV or CVC: kaa H, pon H, niikah HL, yaanii HL, ʔenkaa HL, heekopo HLH, kahkemah HLH) and otherwise on the second syllable (sapa LH, cikah LH, ʔikuu LH, hekaci LHL, ʔarawan LHL, nisahta LHL, ʔuneeno LHL, hacikoo LHL). Pitch is not phonologically distinctive; vowel length carries the contrasts (Itabashi 2001: 90 after Murasaki 1979: 5-6; Hattori & Chiri 1960: 35; Hattori 1961: 5).
4638.srule: In words of more than two morae, secondary accents (副アクセント: lower pitch peaks) fall on the even-numbered morae after the main accent (4th, 6th, 8th mora), each successively lower in pitch; as for the main accent, an accent due on a V mora (second half of a long vowel) or a C* mora (coda /s m n w y h/) shifts to the preceding mora. Examples: sapanuma LHLH (~LLLH), heekopo HLH, kahkemah HLH; hosipire, ʔutasare LHLH. (Itabashi 2001: 90, crediting Murasaki 1979: 5-6.)

Hattori 1961: 5: 'アクセント素は,同数のモーラの上に加わるものは1種である。(いわゆる1型アクセント)。従って,本稿では,アクセント記号は用いない。' The prominence coded here is therefore a predictable pitch peak (phonetic 'pitch accent'), not a stress in the dynamic sense; Itabashi writes the contours syllable by syllable (LH, HL) to compare them with the Hokkaido distinctive accent, which he finds them to match almost entirely (sec. 3.b pp. 91-92).

tn.quote: 本文據此論斷，阿美語重音具詞彙性（lexical stress），即每個詞彙皆帶有一重音，且其結構對應的最小單位為韻律詞（prosodic word）。 … 參照圖七，撒奇萊雅語四類詞尾音節語音皆實現為高降調，顯示其詞彙重音的音韻形式為 H* L𝜔，低調（L𝜔）歸屬於韻律詞邊界。 … 詞彙範疇中最顯著音節穩定落於詞末，即使邊界層級不一，仍不影響其詞尾固定性，顯示阿美語詞彙重音無移位現象，屬「固定位置」的重音語言
tn.translation: We therefore conclude that Amis stress is lexical (lexical stress): every word carries one stress, and its minimal structural unit is the prosodic word. … As Figure 7 shows, in Sakizaya all four word-final syllable types are realised as high-falling, showing that the phonological form of its lexical stress is H* Lω, the low (Lω) belonging to the prosodic-word boundary. … the most prominent syllable in the lexical domain falls stably on the word-final syllable regardless of boundary level, showing that Amis lexical stress does not shift: it is a 'fixed-position' stress language.
